panels.figure_caption: Various presentations of polypoid solitary rectal ulcer syndrome (P‐SRSUS) in the anal canal and rectum: (a, e) Narrow‐band imaging (NBI) views showing the characteristic vascular patterns of polypoid lesions in the rectal and anal canal. These images highlight the altered microvasculature, with capillary loops and irregular vessel distribution indicative of mucosal changes associated with P‐SRSUS. (b, c, f) White‐light endoscopy revealing the surface morphology and color of the rectal and anal canal lesions. Panel (b) demonstrates a large, irregular polyp with a hyperemic surface, while panel (c) shows a nodular lesion with visible mucosal irregularities. Panel (f) presents multiple smaller polypoid formations along the rectal mucosa. (d) Endoscopic ultrasound view displaying the lesion's hypoechoic characteristics and submucosal involvement. This imaging aids in evaluating the depth of invasion and the lesion's relationship with surrounding structures.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Gross specimen photograph from a human patient showing multiple mucous-covered rectal polyps; the article title (Rectal Polyposis in Mucosal Prolapse Syndrome) and in-text statement that the features are consistent with mucosal prolapse syndrome (a synonym of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome) directly attribute this panel to SRUS. The polypoid/multiple-polyp presentation is a recognized less-common (variant) form of the disease rather than the classic solitary ulcer. B: H&E histopathology of the resected rectal polyps from the same human patient, showing granulation tissue with hypertrophic, splayed muscularis mucosa — the classic microscopic features of mucosal prolapse syndrome (solitary rectal ulcer syndrome), as confirmed by the article title and in-text attribution.

in_text_mentions: Gross examination revealed approximately 42 polyps on the mucosal surface (Figure 1A). The largest polyp measured 1.4 cm × 1.0 cm × 0.8 cm. There was no lymph node enlargement in the perirectal tissue. Microscopically, the polyps consisted of granulation tissue with ulcerated surface. There were focal mucosal crypts dilatation, hypertrophic and splayed muscularis mucosa and ectatic submucosal blood vessels (Figure 1B). These features are consistent with mucosal prolapse syndrome. At one-week post-operative follow up, he was well with neither rectal bleeding nor constipation.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Real patient colonoscopy image from a case report of rectal mucosal prolapse syndrome (SRUS). Panel A shows reddened, flat-elevated patchy erythematous lesions on the rectal walls, consistent with polypoid prolapsing mucosal folds of SRUS. The article title and caption directly attribute these rectal lesions to the SRUS spectrum. B: Real patient chromocolonoscopy image after indigo-carmine dye spraying, clearly demonstrating a large shallow ulceration on top of the rectal lesions. This is the classic solitary rectal ulcer of SRUS, directly captioned and supported by the article's focus on rectal mucosal prolapse syndrome.

A patchy erythematous lesion was observed on the right wall of the proximal rectum, and a similar lesion was seen on the left wall of the distal rectum just above the anal verge (Figure 1A). On the top of both lesions, a large shallow ulceration became clearer with a chromocolonoscopy after spraying of indigo-carmine dye (Figure 1B). One lesion showed increased wall thickness with a faint barium fleck, and another showed a nodular flat protrusion with slight deformity of the wall.

panels.rationale: Single sagittal MR defecography image (evacuation phase) from a disease-focused SRUS case report, with a red arrow marking an anterior rectocele. The in-text anchors internal rectal prolapse (internal intussusception) and right-sided rectal wall thickening to Figure 4, framing these defecographic abnormalities as the functional/morphologic basis of repetitive mucosal trauma in this SRUS patient. The arrowed anterior rectocele is not in the allowed vocabulary and is recorded as a proposed finding; internal intussusception is tagged from the in-text phrase tied to this figure. A recognized but less common imaging presentation of SRUS than the classic endoscopic solitary anterior rectal ulcer, hence variant. Age, ethnicity and skin tone are not assessable or not stated.

A: Axial pelvic MRI of the same 29-year-old patient; the disease-focused article title (Rectal Mucosal Prolapse Syndrome mimicking Crohn's disease) plus the captioned manifestation (circumferential wall thickening with a mass-like lesion in the mid-rectum) attributes this rectal wall-thickening/mass presentation to solitary rectal ulcer syndrome rather than the initially suspected Crohn's disease. No vocabulary key matches MRI wall thickening, so it is recorded as proposed findings. B: Colonoscopic view of the patient's rectal lesion: an irregular nodular polypoid prolapsing fold at 5 cm from the anal verge with scant purulent discharge causing a stricture. The polypoid (non-ulcer) form is a recognized less-common presentation of solitary rectal ulcer syndrome, and the article title attributes the case to rectal mucosal prolapse syndrome despite the initial suspicion of Crohn's disease. panels.figure_caption: A 29-year-old male was admitted to the hospital for chronic rectal tenesmus and constipation. Digital rectal examination revealed an immovable and hard mass located 5 cm from the anal verge. Blood tests revealed elevated levels of C-reactive protein and immunoglobulin E. Magnetic resonance imaging revealed circumferential wall thickening with a mass-like lesion in the mid-rectum (A). Colonoscopy showed an irregular nodular lesion at 5 cm from the anal verge with scant purulent discharge adherent to the surface, leading to rectal stricture (B). A mucus-discharging fistula was opening at the center of the lesion ((C,D) white arrow). Initial biopsies revealed chronic inflammation of the mucosa, accompanied by hyperplastic glandular epithelial cells. Based on these findings, a diagnosis of Crohn’s disease (CD) was suspected.
